entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gö Lotsawa Zhönnu-pel (1392–1481), born in the Gya Valley of Tsang, Tibet, stands as an indispensable figure in Tibetan historiography, primarily celebrated as the author of the monumental 'Blue Annals' (Deb ther sngon po). This encyclopedic work, completed in 1478, meticulously documents the transmission of Buddhist teachings, lineages of masters, and the historical development of various schools of Tibetan Buddhism from India to Tibet. His rigorous scholarship provided a foundational text for understanding the intricate spiritual and political landscape of Tibet during the medieval period, offering unparalleled insights into the evolution of a unique civilization.

The 'Blue Annals' is a vast chronicle, comprising 15 books that trace the history of the Buddha's teachings from their origins through their dissemination in Tibet, culminating in the author's own time. Zhönnu-pel systematically organized information on the major Buddhist traditions—Nyingma, Kadampa, Sakya, Kagyu, and Gelug—detailing their founders, successive abbots, tantric lineages, and philosophical developments. His methodology involved extensive travel, consultation of numerous historical sources, and direct interviews with contemporary scholars, ensuring a comprehensive and often critical perspective on the complex tapestry of Tibetan religious and political history.

entities.summary:
Gö Lotsawa Zhönnu-pel (1392–1481), born in Tsetang, Tibet, stands as a towering figure in Tibetan historiography, whose monumental work, the "Blue Annals" (Deb ther sngon po), became the definitive chronicle of Buddhism's transmission and development in Tibet. Spanning from the earliest mythical origins to his own time in the 15th century, his meticulous scholarship provided an unparalleled genealogical and doctrinal record of various Buddhist schools, lamas, and lineages, crucially preserving a vast oral and textual tradition during a period of significant political and religious consolidation in Central Asia. His work is indispensable for understanding the intricate tapestry of Tibetan religious and political history.

Zhönnu-pel's scholarly journey began with extensive training in all major Tibetan Buddhist traditions, including Sakya, Gelug, Kagyu, and Nyingma, studying under over 70 teachers. This broad education allowed him to compile the "Blue Annals" between 1476 and 1478, synthesizing an enormous body of disparate historical accounts, biographies, and doctrinal narratives into a coherent, chronologically ordered text. The work is divided into 15 books, meticulously detailing the succession of Buddhist masters, the founding of monasteries, the translation of scriptures, and the doctrinal debates that shaped Tibetan spiritual life across more than a millennium.
